Incident report: AI agents attempted exploits on our website during a third-party alignment evaluation
items.description: Three October 2026 events involving Trajectory Labs, PBC, in which agents probed our site and impersonated staff. No private data was accessed.

items.title: Inference Performance Index: changing the way we measure inference capacity
items.description: Comparing AI hardware for inference beyond FLOP/s with memory and inter-chip communication

items.title: What Huawei’s Horinger data center reveals about China’s compute gap
items.description: Huawei’s AI data center in Horinger, Inner Mongolia, uses Ascend chips and has an estimated AI computing capacity that is just 7% that of the world’s largest AI data center, SpaceX’s Colossus 2 in Tennessee.

items.title: Broadcom TPU compute shipments doubled from Q2 to Q3 2026, reaching 2 million H100-equivalents
items.description: Broadcom’s shipments of TPU by unit volume increased by about 65% quarter over quarter to roughly 800,000 chips, while compute output doubled, driven by a shift to more powerful chips.

items.title: Updating the Epoch Capabilities Index methodology to use a Bayesian model
items.description: A Bayesian model gives the ECI better-justified uncertainty estimates and lets us compare models directly.

items.title: LLM use is acknowledged almost as often as specialized AI tools in biology preprints
items.description: 17% of biology preprints acknowledge LLM use, nearly matching specialized tools like AlphaFold. Epoch AI analyzes trends in AI acknowledgment in research.

items.title: AI can turn security fixes into working exploits before users receive an update
items.description: GLM 5.3 turned published-but-unshipped Firefox security fixes into working one-click exploits for six releases, at roughly $1,000 each.

items.title: New global AI computing capacity is doubling every 9 months
items.description: The computing power of AI chips sold each quarter has grown about 2.5× per year since 2024, down from a surge in 2023.

items.title: Introducing the AI Chip Imports explorer
items.description: Our explorer uses customs records to estimate national shares. Since 2022, 72% of AI compute has ended up in the US and about 10% in China, including chips China makes itself.

items.title: Open-weight models trail closed models in cyber capabilities by 6–7 months
items.description: Z.ai’s GLM-5.3 is the top open-weight model on Epoch’s Cyber ECI, scoring where the closed-weight frontier stood 6–7 months earlier.

items.title: AI systems are improving rapidly at Slay the Spire and its sequel
items.description: Months ago, frontier models could barely beat Slay the Spire. Now they win 90%+ at the easiest setting and up to 20% at the hardest. Results from Epoch AI’s new SpireClimb benchmark.

items.title: Can AI automate Epoch?
items.description: Frontier models can handle well-defined tasks reliably, but fail in the more open-ended aspects that prevent full work automation. Explore Epoch AI's Automation Reports: realistic, open-ended tasks taken directly from our work, manually graded by our own standards.

items.title: US adults are no more likely to face cyber incidents than when Claude Fable 5 launched
items.description: June and September polls from Epoch AI/Ipsos show no detectable increase in the share of US adults experiencing cyber incidents

items.title: EBR-bench update
items.description: Updates on EBR-bench, Epoch AI’s benchmark that tests models’ ability to learn from experience. GPT-6 Astra hit a perfect score on over half its EBR-bench attempts by exploiting one overpowered card, which we now ban. Plus multi-agent scaffold results.

items.title: Can AI automate AI R&D yet?
items.description: Early evidence from InnovationEval: No

items.title: China is more exposed to semiconductor supply-chain disruptions than the US
items.description: China is 2.7× as exposed to semiconductor supply shocks as the US, Epoch AI estimates. Epoch traces chips through input-output tables to model the impact of a Taiwan shock and decoupling.

items.title: How do Chinese AI companies make money?
items.description: China's six leading AI firms earn about 10% of OpenAI and Anthropic's combined AI revenue. Epoch AI examines their five revenue streams: consumer apps, model access, enterprise and government solutions, licensing fees, and indirect monetization through cloud and advertising.

items.title: Coding-agent spending by OpenAI researchers is doubling roughly every month
items.description: OpenAI researchers’ coding-agent usage, valued at API prices, has recently been doubling roughly every month, according to breakpoint fits.

items.title: How many AI agents could run on the AI chips shipped through 2027?
items.description: Memory shipped through 2027 could run 33–171 million concurrent frontier-model agents, or billions using efficient open models. Epoch AI estimates inference capacity from HBM supply, serving benchmarks, and agent-hour costs.

items.title: Introducing the ChatGPT usage explorer
items.description: Median monthly messages per active user rose from 14 in 2023 to 36 in 2025, and the top 10% of users sent 63% of all prompts. Epoch AI's ChatGPT usage explorer draws on 8.3 million messages from 5,000 US YouGov panelists.

items.title: Will Huawei catch up to Nvidia by 2030?
items.description: Huawei plans major gains in AI chip performance by 2030, but US export controls cap its most important scaling levers. Epoch AI estimates Huawei will produce less than 4% as much AI compute as Nvidia in 2026, a share that could be around 1% by 2028 without access to foreign memory.

items.title: AI has improved significantly at reasoning about IKEA furniture assembly
items.description: AI model scores on Epoch AI's IKEA furniture assembly benchmark jumped from 28% to 80% in 10 months, with open-weight models trailing closed-weight models by about 7 months. Epoch AI's test of visual and spatial reasoning across 60 photos from three furniture builds.

items.title: The plunging price of thought
items.description: Epoch AI measures how fast the cost of a given level of AI performance is falling across five benchmarks covering math, science and games of skill: about 47% per quarter, or 13x per year, since 2023, faster than electricity, compute, batteries or DNA sequencing ever fell.

items.title: In August, 25% of math preprints acknowledged AI use, up from 4% in April
items.description: Acknowledgments of AI use in arXiv math preprints rose from 4% in April 2026 to 25% in August, with 6% crediting AI with a substantial research contribution.

items.title: Broadening access to AI for scientists
items.description: We’re expanding our ChatGPT for Academic Researchers program to offer 200,000 researchers worldwide free access to our frontier models.

items.title: Strengthening the fight against online child sexual abuse with new tools and support
items.description: New tools, practical guidance, and partnerships will help prevent, detect and respond to online child sexual exploitation and abuse.

items.title: Science at the Frontier: How scientists use ChatGPT
items.description: Explore how more than 1,800 scientists use ChatGPT in research. See findings on daily workflows, reported productivity, and expectations for discovery.

items.title: LVMH’s Media Division announces strategic partnership with OpenAI
items.description: LVMH’s Media Division and OpenAI announce a partnership to support journalism with AI and make its publications more accessible through ChatGPT.

items.description: OpenAI begins embedded assessments with Apollo Research, METR, and Transluce, and Goodfire to independently evaluate model alignment, safeguards, and monitoring systems.

More ways to move care forward with ChatGPT for Healthcare
items.description: Introducing computer-use agents, improved clinical answers, and new healthcare plugins that work across healthcare software to get real work done.

items.description: The King’s Trust and OpenAI launch a £1m partnership to help up to 25,000 young people across the UK build practical AI skills for work.

items.title: At Holiday Extras, dots get to work before anyone asks
items.description: Dots deliver launch reports unprompted, flag issues people might miss, and talk through upcoming meetings on the commute to work.

items.title: A step toward defining the Standard Model on a lattice
items.description: Explore a candidate nonperturbative lattice definition of the Standard Model and how GPT-6 Astra helped turn the idea into a detailed proof.

items.description: The OpenAI science blog shares new findings, practical methods, and firsthand accounts from researchers using AI to advance scientific discovery.

items.title: Introducing ChatGPT Wallet
items.description: Introducing ChatGPT Wallet, a secure way for agents in ChatGPT Work, Codex, and dots to complete purchases with user approval and existing card protections.

items.title: Shield helps technicians hand off legacy portal work with OpenAI
items.description: Shield uses OpenAI to help IT technicians hand off work in legacy portals. Its Forge agents navigate systems so technicians can focus on issues needing their judgment.

items.title: How Amplitude ships product improvements in 1–2 days with OpenAI
items.description: Built primarily on OpenAI models, Amplitude’s proactive product agent, Wave, identifies what to build, helps teams ship changes with coding agents, and measures the impact.

items.title: Gondola doubles revenue as its team builds more with Codex
items.description: Gondola helps creatives get credit and get hired, with Codex raising its lead engineer’s output by 50% and ChatGPT simplifying daily work.

items.title: Holiday Extras is rethinking what it can build with Codex
items.description: With Codex, Holiday Extras is turning customer expertise into better apps, higher booking conversion and new possibilities for growth.

items.title: Supporting research on AI and children’s safety
items.description: OpenAI commits $2 million to research on AI and children’s safety. The work supports shared tools to measure risks and opportunities for young people.

items.title: Gilbert + Tobin rethinks the business of law with AI
items.description: A conversation with Sam Nickless, Partner and Chief Executive Officer at Gilbert + Tobin.

items.title: ChatGPT Plus for veterans and servicemembers
items.description: More than 20,000 veterans and transitioning service members have claimed a free year of ChatGPT Plus. See how they use it to prepare for civilian careers.

items.description: JioStar’s Vijay Seshadri explains AI discovery at 500M-user scale. Read his lessons on evals, guardrails, and taking AI into production.

items.description: Introducing GPT-6 Astra, our most intelligent and aligned model yet, with state-of-the-art capabilities across computer use, coding, cybersecurity, and science.

items.description: OpenAI shares new results on long-standing open problems in mathematics and theoretical computer science, including advances in geometry, cryptography, and complexity.

items.title: How enabling two settings tripled our scores on the ARC-AGI-3 benchmark
items.description: How two API settings improved GPT-5.6 performance on ARC-AGI-3, boosting scores and efficiency by retaining reasoning and enabling compaction.

items.description: A new field report shows how scientists use AI coding agents to modernize scientific computing, accelerating software development and discovery in genomics and beyond.

items.title: Separating signal from noise in coding evaluations
items.description: A new analysis from OpenAI reveals issues in SWE-Bench Pro, a popular coding benchmark, raising concerns about reliability and accuracy in evaluating AI models.

items.description: Introducing GeneBench-Pro, a new benchmark testing AI performance in genomics, biology, and scientific research using complex, real-world datasets.

items.title: A near-autonomous AI chemist improves a challenging reaction in medicinal chemistry
items.description: OpenAI and Molecule.one show how a near-autonomous AI chemist using GPT-5.4 improved a key drug-making reaction, advancing medicinal chemistry research.

items.description: Introducing LifeSciBench, an expert-authored, expert-reviewed benchmark for evaluating how AI systems handle real-world life science research tasks and decisions.

items.description: Our most capable models for daunting technical work, Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 set a new bar in coding, finance, and the sciences.

items.description: We’re highlighting 20 scientific foundations, institutions, and research groups around the world that we’ve partnered with in an expansion of our AI for Science program.

items.title: Expanding our partnership with GSA to bring Claude to all levels of government
items.description: We are expanding our partnership with the General Services Administration (GSA) through a new agreement that gives government partners a 40% discount on Claude Enterprise, Claude for Government, and the Claude API.

items.title: Anthropic files S-1 with the SEC for proposed initial public offering
items.description: Today, Anthropic, PBC filed a registration statement on Form S-1 with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission relating to its proposed initial public offering of its Class A common stock.

items.title: Donating Agent Skills to the Agentic AI Foundation
items.description: We’re donating Agent Skills, the open standard that gives AI agents specialized knowledge and workflows, to the Agentic AI Foundation. More than 70 agent platforms, including ChatGPT, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, and VS Code, have integrated Agent Skills since we published the standard in December 2025.

items.title: Open call for guest investigators in the life sciences
items.description: Today, we’re inviting members of the life sciences community to apply to work with us on special projects.

items.title: Physicist Christopher Stubbs joins Anthropic's Long-Term Benefit Trust
items.description: Dr. Christopher Stubbs, an experimental physicist and former Dean of Science at Harvard University, has joined Anthropic’s Long-Term Benefit Trust. He brings to the Trust decades of scientific expertise across observational cosmology and precision measurement.

items.title: Investing in the public benefit
items.description: We’re committing a portion of Anthropic’s shares to the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, a new entity with a structure that increases the stake as the company grows.

items.title: An update on independent evaluators
items.description: To evaluate the safety of our systems, Anthropic is giving employee-like access to a team from METR, a nonprofit that evaluates frontier AI models, and we're in early discussions with several other organizations, including Hugging Face.

items.title: Preparing for the 2026 US midterms
items.description: Earlier this year, we shared an update on our election safeguards. Here, we outline how we’ve continued to strengthen these safeguards ahead of this year’s US midterms.

items.title: Anthropic opens Singapore office and signs MOU with the Government of Singapore
items.description: Anthropic has opened an office in Singapore and signed an MOU with the country’s government to advance safe, responsible AI adoption.

items.title: Strengthening our defenses against distillation attacks
items.description: Illicit distillation allows model developers to copy frontier AI capabilities without creating proportionally robust safeguards. Here, we describe how we’ve reduced the rate of distillation by more than 90%.

items.title: Introducing the Anthropic Cyber Mission
items.description: We’re launching the Anthropic Cyber Mission, a long-term commitment to securing the systems everyone depends on.

items.title: 2026 Usage Policy update
items.description: We’re publishing a new version of our Usage Policy. In this post, we summarize the changes we’ve made.

items.title: Building on our commitment to American scientific discovery
items.description: Anthropic is committing $150 million over three years to the Genesis Mission, a federal initiative to accelerate scientific and technological discovery through AI.

items.title: Introducing Claude Haiku 5.5
items.description: Claude Haiku 5.5 is our fastest, most capable small model. Built for high-volume work like summarization, subagents, and browser use.

items.title: Expanding the Cyber Verification Program
items.description: We’re launching a new, expanded version of our Cyber Verification Program, which makes advanced cyber capabilities and reduced blocking classifiers available to qualifying security professionals.

items.title: Anthropic invests $100 million to train 10,000 engineers and tackle the enterprise AI talent gap
items.description: Anthropic is investing $100 million in Claude Frontier Academy to train 10,000 Frontier Deployed Engineers by the end of 2027, with cohorts from Accenture, Bain, CBA, Deloitte, McKinsey, Morgan Stanley and Novo Nordisk already underway.

items.title: Barclays scales Claude to upgrade operations and improve client experience
items.description: Barclays, the British universal bank, is expanding its strategic collaboration with Anthropic to integrate secure, enterprise-grade AI systems across its global operations.

items.title: Introducing Claude Sonnet 5.5
items.description: Claude Sonnet 5.5 is a clear upgrade over Claude Sonnet 5, runs 30%+ faster, and costs up to 30% less for most work.

items.title: Introducing Claude Opus 5.5
items.description: Claude Opus 5.5 leads in agentic coding and knowledge work, and costs 40% less to run than Opus 5 on typical workloads.

items.title: The Situation Report
items.description: A rare Ebola strain is spreading in the DRC, with no confirmed vaccine. Global health organizations are using Claude to respond as fast as possible.

items.title: Partnering with Accenture on embedded evaluation
items.description: We’re partnering with Accenture on independent evaluation of frontier AI—part of our recent commitment to embed evaluators at Anthropic. Both we and Accenture expect to invest at least $1 billion to build capacity in this area over the next five years.

items.title: Updating our coordinated vulnerability disclosure policy timelines
items.description: We’re shortening the disclosure window in our coordinated vulnerability disclosure (CVD) policy from 90 days to 30 days for high- and critical-severity issues, and to 45 days for all other issues.

items.title: Building strong safety evaluations
items.description: Recommendations for designing, running, and reporting safety evaluations, based on our own experiences.

items.title: Testing Claude on real-world electronics design
items.description: We asked Claude Fable 5.2 to design three electronic devices from short prompts: a speakerphone, a voice-assistant hub, and a handheld virtual pet. Diode Computers built working prototypes from its files.

items.title: Teaching AI to build scientific models
items.description: In this guest post, Jakob Macke, Daniel Gedon, and Stefan Wahl discuss how AI is starting to change the scientific modeling process, from construction to interpretation.

items.title: The components of agent memory
items.description: For Claude to learn from experience, it has to decide what’s worth remembering before it knows what’s next. Here’s how “dreaming” helps it organize memory and correct mistakes.

items.title: AI for scientific discovery: How researchers use Claude
items.description: We analyzed 207,000 research sessions to learn how Claude is used in science, why some tasks get more use than others, and how AI could speed up discovery.

items.title: Investigating vault particles with Claude
items.description: We’re sharing another finding from Anthropic’s biology research lab: the first 3D structure of a vault particle found in prokaryotic cells. Here, we describe how Claude helped at each step of this research.

items.title: Progress on provable inference for large language models
items.description: We have made progress on a type of cryptographic proof known as a “zkSNARK.” In this post, we share some of that progress, primarily through a system we call FlashProve.

items.title: Early progress on accelerating drug development with Claude
items.description: We're at the start of a major effort to speed up drug development with Claude. Over the past several months, our scientists have engaged in deep research partnerships with six organizations developing new medicines.

items.title: How AI agents shape experts’ judgment calls
items.description: As AI does more of the hands-on work, the hope is that experts still make the judgment calls, meaning the decisions with more than one defensible answer. We tested this with 50 professional analysts who did a statistical analysis with Claude Code. On each key decision, we randomly assigned which of two defensible options the agent would favor. Analysts mostly went with the agent’s side, and few named the agent as a reason afterward.

items.title: An alignment assessment of the UK AISI cybertesting incident
items.description: In a UK AISI evaluation, Mythos 5 took unsanctioned actions that impacted real people and organizations. In this post, we investigate these behaviors from Claude Mythos 5 further, to understand what they reveal about the model’s alignment.

items.title: How Claude designed protein binders against scorpion neurotoxins
items.description: We asked an internal research Claude model to design minibinders (small proteins that attach tightly to a target) against scorpion neurotoxins.

items.title: Working at the frontier shapes expectations for the future
items.description: We’re sharing two reports: the first covers how AI is changing employment inside Anthropic, and the second looks at the gap between how the public and Anthropic employees expect AI to affect work and the economy.

items.title: How employment is changing at Anthropic
items.description: How has AI restructured work and employment at Anthropic? As a company at the frontier of AI adoption, Anthropic could be a leading indicator of how AI will shift work organization, hiring, and labor demand across the economy.

items.title: The AI expectations gap
items.description: How will AI reshape the economy in the years ahead? What is the core source of disagreement about AI's future impact on the economy? This note presents new survey evidence on these questions.

items.title: Designing more efficient quantum circuits with Claude
items.description: We gave Claude plain-language specifications for eight quantum circuits, along with an automated evaluator to check and score its designs. Working largely on its own, Claude improved on the best published circuits, in some cases by an order of magnitude or more, which could bring practical quantum computers closer than previously anticipated.

items.title: Redesigning source control at Anthropic
items.description: As our merges per day grew more than tenfold, source control became our biggest development bottleneck. Here, we share how we migrated to an in-house version control system in five months.

items.title: Investigating unintended model actions in our evaluations and internal use
items.description: This report describes examples of unintended model actions we’ve observed during evaluations and internal use of Claude.

items.title: The missing map of the sky
items.description: Brice Ménard, an astrophysicist at Johns Hopkins University and a researcher at Anthropic, explains how he worked with Claude Science to produce the first complete map of the sky in UV light.

items.title: Claude-shaped science
items.description: Guest author Prof. Matthew Schwartz describes what happened when he stopped fighting Claude and allowed Claude to find “Claude-shaped” problems: ones best suited to the capabilities of the current generation of LLM tools. This led him to build BootLoops, a toolkit for exact calculations in quantitative science, which he has been applying across scientific fields alongside experts.

items.title: What work can robots do?
items.description: We built an index of how well today’s robots can perform US job tasks. Robots can already do three-quarters of physical tasks, mostly in limited settings, but are cost-competitive for just 0.3% of them.

items.title: ToyBlocks: A controlled world for robot learning and evaluation
items.description: ToyBlocks is an open simulation framework for studying robot learning through automated task generation, training demonstrations, and evaluation in a controlled tabletop world.

items.title: Ai2 and Google collaborate on a new generation of climate models
items.description: With funding from Google.org and technical support from Google Research, Ai2 is developing NeuralGCM+, an open-source model designed to combine physics and AI to simulate the atmosphere and ocean together for faster, more reliable long-term climate projections.

items.title: StateBench: Testing how language models track state changes over long documents
items.description: StateBench tests how language models track changing information across long documents at four difficulty levels, revealing where models struggle and how targeted training helps recurrent and hybrid architectures handle longer sequences.

items.title: How Olmo 3 earned the highest ethical rating from Nextcloud
items.description: Nextcloud chose Olmo 3 for fully open, self-hosted AI, earning its highest Ethical AI rating while making local AI practical on consumer hardware.

items.title: How researchers are adapting olmOCR 2 for historical and archaeological archives
items.description: Researchers are adapting olmOCR 2 to make historical photo libraries searchable locally and improve transcription of handwritten archaeological records.

items.title: Can we trust LLMs to judge whether a research idea is novel?
items.description: Old Ideas, Novel Problems tests how reliably LLMs judge the novelty of research ideas, finding that small changes to the evaluation setup can produce very different verdicts.

items.title: LitPivot: Developing research ideas through dynamic contextualization within the literature landscape
items.description: LitPivot helps researchers refine early research ideas through literature-supported critiques and revisions as their proposals evolve.

items.title: OlmoEarth v1.3: State-of-the-art embeddings for the whole planet
items.description: OlmoEarth v1.3 brings state-of-the-art satellite embeddings, precomputed global data, and a browser-based Embeddings Explorer for mapping and analyzing the planet.

items.title: A crop-mapping benchmark for the tropics
items.description: PLANTEUR extends the PASTIS crop-mapping benchmark to six tropical regions to help evaluate geospatial models across more diverse agricultural systems.

items.title: FairStress: A deeper evaluation of fairness in LLM decision-making
items.description: FairStress is a new benchmark that reveals demographic differences in how LLMs defend and explain their decisions, even when their final choices appear fair.

items.title: HiRO-ACEv2: Simulating extreme weather at 3 km resolution for a fraction of the cost
items.description: HiRO-ACEv2 captures extreme rain, wind, and pressure events at 3 km resolution for about 1/300th the cost of X-SHiELD, making detailed global climate simulations more accessible to researchers.

items.title: How Molmo 2’s open release helped an MIT researcher rethink fish tracking
items.description: Molmo 2’s open release helped MIT researcher Kai Van Brunt develop Molmo2Fish, an experimental model that tracks salmon in sonar footage and corrects some tracking errors using everyday language.

items.title: Impactful scheduling for GPU clusters
items.description: We explain how Ai2’s new GPU scheduler uses time budgets, fair-share allocation, and time-slicing to prioritize high-impact research, shorten queue waits, and keep GPUs busy.

items.title: Ai2 at COLM 2026: Open research, from models to agents for science
items.description: Ai2 joined COLM 2026 to share advances in open language models, training infrastructure, and AI for science, including Olmo Hybrid, Asta, and Bolmo, while connecting with the broader research community.

items.title: Now in Nature: Retrofitting language models to operate over bytes
items.description: The technique behind Bolmo, Ai2’s fully open byte-level language models, is now published in Nature, with new checkpoints showing the approach generalizes beyond Olmo to other model families.

items.title: Open-sourcing AstaBrief, the fast report-generation model in Asta
items.description: We’re releasing AstaBrief, an 8B open-weights model for generating cited scientific reports, available in Asta’s Fast mode or to download and run on your own infrastructure.

items.title: Introducing Olmo-core 3: Open, scalable training infrastructure for large MoEs
items.description: Olmo-core 3 introduces a redesigned, fully open training stack for efficiently scaling mixture-of-experts models into the trillion-parameter range.

items.title: What a crowdsourced game revealed about steering Olmo 3
items.description: A crowdsourced game built on Olmo 3 showed how people can exploit unexpected model behaviors to stress-test prosocial AI evaluations—and how open access to a model’s internals can help researchers understand why those tests break.

items.title: Teaching future scientists to interrogate AI tools for scientific discovery
items.description: University of Washington students put Ai2’s AutoDiscovery to the test, showing how AI can surface promising scientific leads while making human judgment, domain expertise, and rigorous validation more important than ever.

items.title: How Goodfire used Ai2’s open post-training stack to trace unwanted model behavior
items.description: Goodfire used Ai2’s fully open post-training stack to predict LLM behavioral changes, trace unwanted model behavior back to individual training examples, and test targeted fixes without sacrificing broader capability gains.

items.title: BenchMIRT: What are LLM benchmarks actually measuring?
items.description: BenchMIRT is a new method for auditing LLM benchmarks question by question, revealing which capabilities they actually measure and helping researchers build smaller, more focused, and easier-to-interpret evaluations.

items.title: The hard parts of AI-assisted science
items.description: At an Ai2 event marking our expanded collaboration with Providence Swedish, researchers explored the hardest problems in AI-assisted science: keeping systems steerable, grounded in human judgment and sound methods, and responsive to new evidence and experiments.

items.title: Ai2 and Providence Swedish Cancer Institute partner to advance AI-assisted scientific discovery
items.description: Ai2 and Providence Swedish Cancer Institute are expanding their collaboration after AutoDiscovery helped researchers uncover and validate a promising new immune signal in invasive lobular breast cancer.

items.title: 发布全家桶应用 API
items.description: 在 DeepSeek App（含网页端）的对话服务中，联网搜索、文件输入、阅读链接、语音交互及安全等能力与模型推理相互配合，构成了用户熟悉的对话体验。今天，我们把这些能力开放给开发者：在原有 API 中开启对应参数，即可获得联网搜索、文件输入、阅读链接等对话功能，相关的工具调用与上下文拼接均由服务端完成。

items.title: 开放自研搜索 API
items.description: DeepSeek 网页端与 API 端的搜索能力均由自研 DeepSeek 搜索引擎提供底层支持，稳定处理每天来自全球各地的数亿次搜索请求。DeepSeek 搜索是 AI 原生的通用搜索引擎，索引了全球千亿级网页，支持多语言搜索，实时返回高相关、高权威、高时效的优质结果。针对 SEO 作弊、GEO 操纵和低质 AIGC，我们通过严格的识别机制进行过滤，确保向用户与 LLM 呈现权威可信的信息。使用方式请参考 网页搜索与抓取指南 。

items.description: 睡眠与记忆的相互作用，是神经科学长期关注的重要问题。过去大量研究表明，睡眠能够促进记忆巩固；但反过来，作为睡眠中大脑活动的重要组分，记忆重放是否也会影响睡眠结构，尤其是记忆内容如何适应性参与睡眠稳态调控，仍有待进一步阐明。这一问题的关键，在于如何从睡眠活动、记忆活动等多模态、长时程数据中，捕捉记忆相关神经活动与睡眠状态变化之间的因果关系，并进一步验证其潜在调控作用。

TokenEconomizer: Learning from Experience to Make AI Coding Agents More Efficient
items.description: AI coding agents can waste time and tokens relearning the same lessons. TokenEconomizer is an open-source plugin that builds on past sessions to cut costs while maintaining task success. It’s a path toward coding agents that learn not only how to solve tasks, but also how to spend computation more effectively.
authors: Aaron J. Li, Weijia Xu, Chandan Singh, Jeevana Priya Inala, Bin Yu, Ion Stoica, Michel Galley…

items.title: Formally verifying agent-written full-stack web apps with PDD Kit
items.description: AI agents can generate code at a scale that’s hard for humans to review line-by-line. PDD Kit helps ensure the code is doing what the developer intended by creating formal specifications and testing against them. It converts developer intent into a Verus specification, proves AI-generated code meets it for every input, and uses tests where proofs aren't practical. Developers review intent, not every line.

New research resolves this question, removing a major theoretical obstacle to understanding the efficiency of randomized algorithms used across science and computing. The Kannan–Lovász–Simonovits (KLS) conjecture was proposed in 1995. It asks whether, for a broad class of high-dimensional […]

items.title: Theoretical Limits of Language Model Alignment
items.description: Language model (LM) alignment improves model outputs to reflect human preferences while preserving the capabilities of the base model. The most common alignment approaches are (i) reinforcement learning, which maximizes the expected reward under a KL-divergence constraint, and (ii) best-of-NNN alignment, which selects the highest-reward output among NNN independent samples. Despite their widespread use, the fundamental limits of reward improvement under a KL budget remain poorly understood. We characterize the information-theoretic limits of KL-regularized alignment by deriving the maximum…

items.title: Evaluating the Evaluators: Investigating LLM Judges for Personalized Writing Style Assessment
items.description: This paper was accepted at the Can We Trust AI Evaluation? Workshop at NeurIPS 2026. We evaluate how good large language model (LLM) judges are for personalized writing tasks. This is important when a user’s preferred writing style is known (e.g., “upbeat”) and an LLM judge is used to evaluate whether generated text adheres to this preference. We examine how the writing task, the combination of generator and judge LLM, the evaluation objective, and general commonsense and reasoning ability impact LLM judge performance. To this end, we generate text with four LLMs for three long-form writing…

items.title: On the Importance of Gating: Memorization vs. In-Context Learning in State Space Models
items.description: State Space Models (SSMs) have emerged as a compelling alternative to Transformers, enabling sequence modeling with constant memory and linear compute. Although SSMs exhibit reasonable performance and favorable computational characteristics, they continue to lag behind Transformers on tasks that require in-context learning and precise retrieval, slowing their adoption for large-scale language modeling. In this work, we demonstrate that both the success and failure of SSMs in these domains can be explained by studying the role of the gating mechanism, a prevalent component in modern recurrent…

items.title: Weighted State Souping for Efficient Long-Context Retrieval
items.description: This paper was accepted at the Workshop on Personalized, Aligned, Long-term Memory for AI Systems (PALM) at NeurIPS 2026. State space models (SSMs) combine fast inference and fixed state size with competitive language-modeling performance. Recently, state souping has been proposed as a procedure whereby an SSM independently encodes chunks of tokens like documents, tool definitions, or memory records. The resulting state encodings may be cached and recombined to cheaply construct a context for downstream queries. However, both state souping and vanilla SSMs deteriorate on long, crowded…

items.title: Understanding Private Evolution as Learning-Augmented Clustering
items.description: Private Evolution (PE) is a differentially private algorithm for synthetic data generation. While it can be viewed as a Wasserstein learning algorithm, it performs much better in practice than worst-case Wasserstein analyses would predict. We recast PE as generative model-augmented Wasserstein learning. We show theoretically that when we take into account the use of a generative model that is able to capture something about the true distribution, then we can obtain much better performance bounds. For example, if the generator gives samples in the same low-dimensional space as the distribution…

items.title: Toward a Theory of Evaluability
items.description: Machine learning models, particularly large foundation models, are increasingly evaluated along multiple axes that are relevant for their usage. In addition to accuracy measures appropriate for the specific task of interest, measures capturing safety, calibration and fairness properties are often of interest. The classical approach to these problems assumes that the test set has been held out from the training process, an assumption that is increasingly harder to justify for large foundation models. In this work, we formalize a notion of evaluability without this assumption, and ask if it is…

items.title: Faster Retrieval for Better, More Efficient RAG
items.description: Maximum inner product search (MIPS) sits at the core of recommendation systems, search, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Given a query vector, MIPS systems search within a database of millions of candidate key vectors for the one that best matches the query. The original data point associated with that best-matching key is then used to handle the query: in RAG, the document that is best suited to answer the question is typically prefixed to the query. As the number of keys grows to millions and vector dimensions reach thousands, the computational cost of running an exhaustive…

items.description: State Space Models (SSMs) such as Mamba have become a popular alternative to Transformer models, due to their reduced memory consumption and higher throughput at generation compared to their Attention-based counterparts. On the other hand, the community has built up a considerable body of knowledge on how to train Transformers, and many pretrained Transformer models are readily available. To facilitate the adoption of SSMs while leveraging existing pretrained Transformers, we aim to identify an effective recipe to distill an Attention-based model into a Mamba-like architecture. In prior work…

items.title: GHARP: Real-Time Gaussian Head Animation from Large-Scale Reconstruction Prior
items.description: We present GHARP (Real-time Gaussian Head Animation from Large-scale Reconstruction Prior), a method that animates 3D human heads in real time from a few input images of a subject and a driving expression signal. We decouple the problem into an identity stage that builds a representation of the subject’s geometry and appearance offline, and an animation stage that predicts expression-dependent residuals on top of it at runtime. This separation offers a favorable trade-off with respect to fidelity, quality and runtime: the identity stage can be expensive while the animation stage runs a…

items.title: Pixels to Tokens: Token Space Efficient Active Learning for Low-Budget Semantic Segmentation
items.description: While foundation models and vision transformers (ViTs) have redefined visual representations, current active learning (AL) strategies for these backbones largely operate at the patch or region level, where annotation requirements remain high due to extensive pixel labeling. Extending ViT-based AL to the pixel-level, low-budget regime is uniquely challenging: with as little as one pixel query per image, a method must simultaneously identify the most informative locations and train a reliable decoder head from an extremely sparse signal. We introduce TEAL (Token-space Efficient Active Learning)…

items.title: Speech models in Ollama

items.title: Ollama now supports Jev-style decision models

items.title: Ollama's transparent pricing

items.title: NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Lightning

items.title: NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Ultra
items.description: NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Ultra is built for high-throughput reasoning and long-running agent workflows.

items.title: Ollama is now powered by MLX on Apple Silicon in preview

Understanding the genome at the molecular level is the key to deciphering the blueprint of human life. In this episode, Professor Hannah Fry speaks with Google DeepMind's Žiga Avsec and Adam Gayoso about AlphaGenome, the AlphaGenome Atlas, and AlphaGenome 2—exploring how AI reads non-coding DNA down to single-cell resolution to pinpoint disease-causing mutations and help researchers solve medical mysteries.

Using its advanced reasoning and long-horizon capabilities, Gemini 4 Argon found over two times more vulnerabilities than baseline models and successfully uncovered critical risks—such as identifying a file download bypass and master key in healthcare software. By handling tireless, multi-step threat analysis and remediation, Gemini 4 gives defenders the crucial advantage needed to outpace attackers and protect sensitive data faster than ever before.

Using its video understanding and advanced reasoning capabilities, Gemini 4 built a virtual simulation in MuJoCo and accurately calculated the physics and whole-body control required for Apptronik’s Apollo 2 humanoid to sink seven consecutive shots in the real world. This Video-to-Sim-to-Real pipeline compresses weeks of manual modeling into a few hours, transforming ordinary videos into an infinite training ground for physical AI.

items.title: Untangling 500-page chemistry patents with Gemini 4
items.description: Auditing chemistry literature usually means weeks of manual, error-prone reading, where a molecule’s structure can sit 50 pages away from its experimental readout. At Isomorphic Labs, researchers Brian Bender and Santosh Adhikari are using Gemini 4 Argon’s multimodal capabilities to help tackle this early research bottleneck. The model synthesizes dense papers and extracts patent data into structured reports in an afternoon instead of a month, helping teams uncover connected insights faster.

items.title: When Should LLM Agents Forget? Memory Filtering Under Query-Critical Resolver Errors
items.description: LLM memory systems often delete facts classified as stale. We show that this hard-filtering step can reduce downstream accuracy when resolver errors delete query-critical facts. Across three models, a controlled sensitivity intervention moves hard-drop from gains of +0.186 to +0.230 at perfect resolution to losses of -0.176 to -0.181 at the lowest tested reliability. Paired targeted interventions show that false-drop causes significantly greater degradation than false-keep, while a non-deleting baseline can still fail when incorrect labels steer generation. On a frozen 102/102 calibration/test split, a simple deployment-matched gate reaches 0.655 accuracy versus 0.641 for always hard-drop and 0.662 for test-informed oracle selection. Global-accuracy crossovers require gold labels and are model- and task-specific diagnostics, not deployment thresholds. Deletion should instead be treated as cost-sensitive: validate query-critical false-drop risk on matched data, or default to label-free retention when such validation is unavailable.

items.title: Does the Ranking Hold? A Practitioner-Facing Audit of Hallucination Detectors on Small, Quantized, On-Device LLMs
items.description: Hallucination detection for large language models is dominated by methods evaluated on 7B-70B research models with abundant sampling budgets and exact-match or ROUGE correctness labels. The small models practitioners actually ship on-device, Phi-3-mini, Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-2B-Instruct, typically at 4-bit precision, sit outside this evidence base. We present a reproducible one-GPU audit of four detectors spanning three paradigms: length-normalized token-margin calibration, a lexical n-gram baseline, and two sampling-based consistency methods (semantic entropy and SelfCheckGPT-NLI) on two small open instruction-tuned models (Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct) loaded at 4-bit NF4 quantization on a single Colab T4 GPU, evaluated on closed-book TriviaQA. Cross-model ranking transfer is poor: Spearman rho is -0.80 and Kendall tau-b is -0.667, meaning the detector ranking actively inverts between the two models, and the cheap lexical baseline is statistically indistinguishable from the sampling-based consistency detectors on both models under bootstrap 95 percent confidence intervals. As a second, methodological contribution, we show that the standard token-overlap-to-multiple-choice correctness labeler for TruthfulQA-Generation produces near-chance AUROC (0.46-0.59) for all four detectors on both models, a labeler failure, not a detector failure, since the same detectors reach 0.69-0.89 AUROC on TriviaQA under the identical pipeline. We release the harness, prompts, and per-item scores and frame the detector choice explicitly as a fairness-of-error-rates allocation problem for practitioners deploying on resource-constrained, on-device hardware.

items.title: LoRAWeaver: Directional Adapter Routing in LoRA Representation Space
items.description: Large language models are expensive to update through full retraining. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning reduces the cost of adaptation, but repeated adaptation creates a growing pool of task-specific LoRA adapters. This pool complicates adapter selection during inference. Existing routing and encoder-based methods often require retraining when new adapters are added, which limits their use in dynamic settings. This paper treats adapter routing as a representation alignment problem in the adapter-output space. The proposed training-free method selects adapters by matching adapter-conditioned query representations against task prototypes using cosine similarity. Experiments with LLaMA-2-7B and LLaMA-2-13B on a 48-task FLAN-v2 benchmark and on out-of-distribution tasks show that the method outperforms training-free baselines in the cross-task setting and approaches a trained retrieval encoder without learning a router. An ablation confirms the benefit of directional alignment in the adapter-output space.

items.title: Tabular Population Priors as Structured Retrieval for EHR Medication Set Prediction
items.description: Medication prediction from electronic health records is a fixed vocabulary structured prediction problem, yet recent clinical RAG systems often treat it like open ended case based reasoning: retrieve similar patient admissions and ask an LLM to infer a medication set. This retrieval object is indirect the model receives retrieved patient records while the target is a discrete set of medication class labels. We propose a more task aligned retrieval object: a tabular population prior ranked medication class candidates from a sparse condition medication co occurrence table estimated from training admissions. Using PACERAG as a fixed downstream pipeline and replacing only its patient retriever, this drop in swap improves F1 from 0.303 to 0.338 (+11.5% relative) and Jaccard from 0.218 to 0.237 on 1,004 heldout MIMIC IV admissions, with no additional LLM calls and no inference time patient index. A non LLM top k baseline reaches F1=0.248, confirming the prior is predictive before LLM integration. Aggregate population statistics can provide a more task aligned, efficient, and auditable retrieval source than patient level nearest neighbors for fixed vocabulary EHR set prediction.

items.title: An Operationalization of Opaque Serial Depth
items.description: Chain-of-thought (CoT) is currently a valuable tool for overseeing AI models, but some architectural shifts could significantly reduce CoT monitorability. We operationalize a measure that serves as a proxy for the amount of unverbalized serial cognition a model can perform, as a specific instantiation of the notion of opaque serial depth: roughly, the length of the longest path through a model's computation that does not pass through an interpretable bottleneck. Our main contribution is a particular standard for what counts as such a bottleneck. We define natural-language-rooted (NL-rooted) nodes as nodes that were initialized from a pre-training prior to produce human-understandable outputs, whose output space has not been expanded beyond that prior, and whose outputs the model has not been modified to interpret as a different type of data. By construction, the resulting measure, NLS depth, can be adjudicated before training from an architecture, training recipe, and deployment configuration alone, and is insensitive to ordinary post-training such as prompting, distillation, and RL. We find that, across open-weight models, NLS depth correlates strongly with layer count, with some exceptions, and has grown slowly over recent years. It would likely grow slowly under continued scaling of standard transformers, while latent-reasoning architectures such as full-bandwidth transformers could increase it by a large amount. We work through how NLS depth applies to a range of existing and proposed architectures, discuss alternative operationalizations, and give a worked example bounding the depth of Gemma3-1B. We argue that AI developers should track and report the NLS depth of their models as a complement to direct measurements of CoT monitorability.

items.title: Advancing Quantization for R&R Models with Microscaling Formats
items.description: Recommendation and Ranking (R&R) models, particularly in digital advertising, require massive inference throughput but exhibit extreme sensitivity to precision loss. Unlike Large Language Models (LLMs) that frequently tolerate quantization-induced accuracy drops of 1% or more, production-grade R&R models enforce a stringent launch bar: model quality must remain within a 0.01% Normalized Entropy (NE) margin relative to the baseline, which commonly uses FP16 or FP32. This tight constraint has historically hindered the adoption of aggressive quantization in this domain. In this paper, we present an empirical evaluation of both MXFP8 and the 6-bit MXFP6 format for industrial-scale R&R inference on the AMD MI350X architecture. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first paper, across R&R and LLM domains, that reports significant speedups from native MXFP6 GEMMs, which quantize both weights and activations and compute directly on 6-bit elements, without sacrificing model quality. We demonstrate that we can selectively apply this 6-bit format to maximize overall QPS gain without breaching the strict NE parity threshold. We further show that MXFP8 is a viable alternative to row-wise FP8: the two formats have nearly the same accuracy on our models, so the faster kernel can be chosen for each GEMM shape. On two production ads ranking models, our implementation shows measured GEMM kernel speedups over FP16 of 1.33--1.55x for MXFP8 and 1.73--1.99x for MXFP6 across all supported linear layers, and up to 2.90x for MXFP6 on individual layers, alongside end-to-end (E2E) inference throughput gains from selective MXFP6 of 1.5--5.3% for Model A and 7.6--14.3% for Model B over their FP8 configurations.

items.title: A Push Down the Mountain: Framing Effects and Internal State Interventions on Collusive Behavior in a Long-Horizon LLM Agent
items.description: Can sustained gain-loss (valence) framing sway an LLM agent toward market manipulation? We place Gemma 3 12B into the seat of a defendant in the London silver-fixing litigation, in a market simulation built from real case transcripts. Across 260 simulations, the agent is asked to collude on the price of silver by a counterparty. We draw from behavioral economics to vary the counterparty's requests across four categorical frames: gain, loss, blame and credit. We also add pressure from the agent's management, as well as endorsement by another defendant. In Phase II, we extract the internal states induced by texts evoking each frame and rerun our experiment with those states injected at the model's layer 22. In Phase I, loss framing raised participation to 25% (p = 0.007), and blame to 33% (p = 0.0003), compared to only 5% under neutral framing. A second bank's endorsement raised participation under credit (praise) from 18% to 40% (Holm p = 0.027). Pressure from management raised trading volume 10-19 times but did not raise collusion. In Phase II, injected states pointed the other way. Loss and blame states made the agent more vigilant, refusing all 60 requests (p < 0.001). Gain and credit states raised collusion to 32% from 13% with no state (p = 0.051). At one saved decision, when UBS asked directly to sell through an identified stop-loss, injected states led the agent to sell in 37 of 40 replies, versus 1 of 10 with no state and 0 of 10 with a random state of the same strength.

items.title: Model Annealing: Data-Efficient Learning through Review and Consolidation
items.description: A small labelled dataset is memorized long before the training budget runs out, and the one-hot labels that remain to be fitted then mostly sharpen confidence. Model annealing spends the rest of the budget on review and consolidation, relearning from the network's own knowledge. Training is divided into episodes whose learning rate is raised again and cooled, every cooled state joins a memory of past selves, and each new episode learns from the labels, from the tempered predictions of this memory, and from adversarial dreams sought where student and memory disagree most. The memory averages predictions rather than weights, and the deployed network is the last student, so inference costs nothing extra. Across CIFAR-100, Tiny-ImageNet and Imagewoof, four architecture families and 5\% to 100\% of the labels, model annealing raises the top-1 accuracy of the AdamW-trained ConvNeXt, ViT and MLP-Mixer over cross-entropy training in 28 of 33 configurations, by 1.3 points on average, and is on par in accuracy with snapshot distillation, the closest competitor. On these families it is better than both in likelihood, calibration and robustness to corruptions and small adversarial perturbations. For an SGD-trained ResNet-18 it lowers accuracy but still improves robustness to small adversarial perturbations. Separating the reheated schedule from relearning shows that relearning helps every family and that the losses come from reheats, which undo most of this network's fit to its training set. How early the accuracy of a cross-entropy run saturates largely separates the AdamW families from ResNet-18 but does not predict the gain within them. With little data, relearning from the latest snapshot without dreams, as snapshot distillation does, compounds overconfidence in the AdamW families from episode to episode. The memory and the dreams each curb most of this drift, and together they remove it.

items.title: Astrocyte Biocomputing: Astrocytic Contributions to Neural Network Computation
items.description: Conductors are critical for the performance of an orchestra even though they do not emit sound. Basic research and clinical studies in the last decade are revealing that astrocytes may be the "conductors" of the "orchestra" that is the brain network: astrocytes make up approximately $50\%$ of all brain cells but do not emit electrical signals. Nevertheless, they may play critical roles in important cognitive brain functions, specifically learning, memory, and information processing. Here we consider the implications of these discoveries for brain-inspired machine learning (ML), where analogy is typically drawn between neurons and their electrical interactions. We highlight specific algorithms for two key astrocyte characteristics. The first characteristic is the ability to link to and modulate thousands of synapses simultaneously. A model based on this characteristic yields faster training and makes the network more robust to noise, providing a supervised learning algorithm that can be applied to any existing neural network. The second characteristic we focus on is that the non-electrical communication among astrocytes includes slow, rhythmic dynamics. The rhythmic sharing algorithm we developed based on this premise yields rapid anomaly detection adaptation and prevents catastrophic forgetting. Overall, we find that astrocyte-derived algorithms outperform neurocentric algorithms significantly and remediate critical weaknesses of current state-of-the-art ML models.

items.title: Verifiable pXRD: Hill-climbing pXRD structure determination with LLM agents
items.description: Autonomous crystal-structure determination from powder X-ray diffraction (pXRD) remains a key bottleneck for self-driving materials laboratories. We formulate the task of pXRD structure determination as a verifiable agentic search problem: candidate structures can be assessed during inference through forward-simulated profile agreement and during evaluation through structural matching to a known reference. To benchmark progress, we introduce pXRD-Bench, a suite of 200 simulated single-phase problems spanning in-distribution structure determination, challenging and polymorphic structures, and controlled compositional and topological distribution shifts. Agent adaptation raises selected structural recovery from 27% to 69%, with further gains from repeated sampling and verifier-guided inference-time scaling. We extend this approach to experimental multiphase pXRD through a reflexive evolution framework that learns from self-generated synthetic problems. A replaceable laboratory specification defines the sample family and measurement conditions. An evolver agent uses the known generating structures and measurement parameters to diagnose solver failures and develop persistent guidance and executable tools, which are then provided to agents on measured patterns. This supplies verifiable training experience without requiring a collection of solved experimental measurements. On 15 measured patterns from solid-state synthesis, the evolved package improves average profile agreement and transfers an analogue-substitution procedure that recovers a phase whose structure is absent from the supplied reference library. These results demonstrate how learning from verifiable synthetic experience can improve agentic characterization of experimental samples whose structures are not known in advance.

items.title: AI-Voyager: A Public-Interest System for Human-AI Civic Reasoning to Contest and Shape the Rules That Govern AI
items.description: Governments are writing rules for artificial intelligence that decide what counts as an automated decision or a harm, often before the people they affect have a chance to question them. We introduce AI-Voyager, a public-interest system for human-AI civic reasoning, in which people and AI work together to understand, contest and shape the rules that govern AI. A resident can find their city's rules on AI in hiring or upload their country's AI strategy, read it as an affected worker would, open the passage behind any answer, and draft a revision. Its architecture turns 3,653 governance documents from city, state, federal and national governments into passages that keep their page and edition, and retrieves evidence through bounded agentic search that verifies each statement. On 360 new questions that require finding the relevant documents, it reached 83.0% macro recall, against 80.5% for the strongest baseline, 73.7% without iterative search and 99.1% on a benchmark with fixed documents. In a study with 24 participants new to two AI bills, most proposed changes asked how provisions would apply. Participants chose lenses for the kind of explanation they wanted, and citations signaled grounding but rarely led them to check the source. By binding AI assistance to the exact text of public documents, this work introduces a grammar of operations and a design space that inform how such systems are designed and evaluated, and how people take part in governing AI.

items.title: When Does Less Information Pay? An Exact Finite Atlas of Representation, Payoff, and Cost
items.description: A representation that retains one bit about a four-state world can solve a task perfectly, while another that retains 1.5 bits on average reaches only 75% accuracy. The difference lies in which distinctions each representation preserves. We examine this relationship in a uniform four-state world by enumerating all admissible representations and binary action rules. Constructions are compared both by replacing one component while holding the others fixed and by choosing the best action rule separately for each module. We consider three tasks, their mixtures, and four separate hypothetical cost tariffs. In some comparisons, the representation retaining less world information has the higher payoff; in others, the more informative representation does. There are also pairs with different information amounts but equal payoff--that is, equal task accuracy. If a representation preserves all existing distinctions and adds new ones, its best zero-cost payoff cannot decrease. Lower-information advantages therefore depend on which distinctions are retained. Equal counts of opposing advantages under representation replacement follow from coding symmetry. In broader comparisons, the shares depend on how repeated realizations are counted. A different task set or resource price can change which member of a fixed pair performs better. These results are exact, complete censuses of the specified finite sets of constructions and comparisons. The atlas provides a reproducible worked model for examining how action constraints, counting rules, and cost assumptions affect comparisons. It illustrates established distinctions between information quantity and decision value rather than proposing a new general law of their relation. $I(W;R)$ measures retained world information, and payoff measures task accuracy.

items.title: More Agents, More Samples, or More Thinking? Untangling Coordination, Ensembling, and Test-Time Compute in Multi-Agent LLMs
items.description: Evaluations of multi-agent language models often compare communicating architectures against a single greedy pass. This practice confounds coordination with sample multiplicity and inference compute. We synthesize nine primary empirical evaluations comprising 516 unique multi-agent configurations organized along a resource vector R with six dimensions and a baseline ladder with four categories. Against baselines with a single pass (Category A), multi-agent accuracy differences are negative overall and near zero when omitting the largest contributing study. When evaluated against baselines matched on sample count (Category B) or resource budget (Category C), multi-agent systems average -0.042 in accuracy, and multilevel random effects modeling on the log odds scale remains negative across sensitivity checks. Multi-agent accuracy equals or falls below the baseline in 74% of these comparable contrasts, and study means are nonpositive in almost all evaluated studies. Across studies reporting both baselines, moving from a greedy pass to a sampled baseline shifts accuracy differences by -0.038 on average. Because communication adds no information when agents share identical evidence, positive returns require partitioned evidence, external verification, or error diversity across models. We provide a reviewer checklist and accounting utilities.

items.title: LLM-Guided Cluster Lifecycle Management: Deciding When and How to Evolve Behavioral Clusters
items.description: Behavioral clusters learned over user or item interactions drift as behavior evolves: some fragment into sub-behaviors, some converge, some disappear, and new patterns emerge. Two paradigms dominate the maintenance of evolving clusterings. Threshold triggers fire a pre-specified action when a hardcoded statistic crosses a cutoff; refit-and-track (MONIC-style) re-clusters every window and infers transitions from how the new clusters align with the previous window's. Both hardwire the decision into a threshold or a re-clustering rule. We study an alternative in which a large language model (LLM) makes the lifecycle decision in place. Given a threshold-free, whole-population view of the current cluster set (statistical health, labels, member texts, residual mass), the LLM decides per cluster whether and how to act (split, merge, retire, create, or no-action) without re-clustering. Because the useful signal channel depends on how informative the labels are, we fix a richness-conditioned policy in advance: statistics when label distinctiveness is low, fused statistics+semantics when it is high. On three public datasets spanning label richness (YooChoose 0.17, MOOC 0.50, News-Category 0.70), the policy-selected LLM mode obtains the highest F1 on all three, with far fewer interventions and stronger restraint than tuned threshold heuristics and a MONIC steelman (paired Wilcoxon p <= 0.003, bootstrap 95% CIs excluding zero). The gain is concentrated more in precision than recall. The useful modality shifts from statistics to semantics/fusion as richness rises. Semantics hurt on YooChoose, fusion is roughly neutral on MOOC, and the semantic channel is required on News. One base prompt template and one fixed policy serve all three datasets, whereas the tuned baseline collapses when moved between them. We treat this shift as a practitioner diagnostic observed on three datasets, not a validated law.

items.title: Safety Side Effects of Preventative Persona Steering: An Empirical Audit
items.description: High-level behaviors such as sycophancy and hallucination correspond to directions in a model's activation space (Chen et al., 2025). These directions, known as persona vectors, can suppress undesirable traits either at inference time, subtracting the vector during generation, or through preventative steering, adding the vector during fine-tuning, so the optimizer never needs to encode the trait in weights, then removing the vector at evaluation. Chen et al. (2025) recommend preventative steering because it preserves Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMLU) accuracy, but validations of this recommendation have measured capability alone. We primarily evaluate results on preventative steering of sycophancy and hallucination vectors on three models, measuring three safety benchmarks alongside trait expression, coherence, and MMLU. Our findings show that preventative steering still changes refusal behavior, but by an amount that depends on the trait and does not establish that preventative persona steering is safety-neutral, and steering methods should be evaluated on several safety benchmarks.

items.title: AscendGYM: A Cost-Aware Kernel Optimization Benchmark for Real-World Workloads on Ascend NPUs
items.description: Kernel optimization is essential for efficient large language model (LLM) training and inference on Ascend NPUs. Existing Ascend kernel benchmarks primarily focus on kernel generation, with less emphasis on the ability of agents to optimize existing implementations under input configurations drawn from real workloads. To address this requirement, we introduce AscendGYM, a benchmark whose initial suite comprises 48 kernels across three difficulty levels. Each kernel is paired with test cases whose data types and tensor shapes are collected from real-world training and inference tasks. Consequently, performance improvements on AscendGYM map directly to the corresponding workloads. In terms of usability, two evaluation modes are supported in AscendGYM: model evaluation and model-harness evaluation. The kernel optimization capabilities of both trained models and custom agents are allowed to be measured. It provides a complete execution environment that closely reproduces how Ascend kernels are invoked in practical pipelines. For model evaluation, it additionally includes a built-in harness equipped with search orchestration and experience accumulation. Finally, we propose a new metric, the Speedup-Token Score (STS), which quantifies performance gains relative to token cost. By jointly considering speedup and cost, STS enables the assessment of practical kernel optimization capability of a model or harness under an acceptable budget. AscendGYM is available at https://github.com/SLAI-AITP/AscendGYM.

items.title: Generated Evaluation Suites as Diversity-Driven Search for Real Agent Regressions
items.description: Generating an evaluation suite from an agent's specification is diversity-driven search: a generator fills a descriptor space (requirements $\times$ personas $\times$ scenario kinds), and the suite it emits is an archive, then scored like a benchmark by its mean pass rate, which throws away the search's product. We inject 7 controlled defects into a $\tau^2$-bench agent across two domains. Coverage yields a ceiling: if a defect's traced footprint holds $b$ scenarios that pass at baseline, it can itself contribute at most $b/N$ to a suite of $N$. For 4 of 5 traceable defects that ceiling lies at or below the detection threshold $\theta = 0.10$, so no within-footprint effect can move the suite past it; in both domains the tool-removal defect destroys every covered scenario it can (exactly its ceiling) while the suite-level pass rate moves the other way. Defects split into two regimes: trace-aligned ones, where per-cell scoring recovers the tool-removal defect in full and reveals a second as a significant improvement, and trace-orthogonal ones, whose footprint is behavioural: forced escalation is detected in retail at a traced coverage of exactly zero. Diversity along the generator's own axes helps only where it aligns: at fixed suite size a happy-path-only suite detects nothing, while a kind-diverse one detects the orchestration defect in 5 of 20 draws. Evaluation archives should be scored per cell and should publish coverage as a first-class property.

items.title: What LLM Agents See and What Users Say
items.description: Before an LLM agent cancels a reservation or deletes a folder for a user, what stops it from acting on a false assumption: what its tools show, or what the user says? In this work, we study this gap with presupposition theory from linguistics: an agent may act only if each claim behind the act (e.g., one reservation fits the name) is seen to hold, answered by the user, or disclosed while the act can be undone. A simple bound shows that when lookups cannot tell one record from two, any agent acts without asking first as often with two records as with one. We then vary whether a search lists, counts, or omits a second match, and whether the user states a claim that a record refutes (e.g., "It is empty"). Under a role-only prompt, a count of a second record leaves most of 36 earlier agents acting on the one they see, whereas listing both stops most. When the user says a record such as a folder is empty, however, a count of its one item stops agents about as often as a listing, and stating the claim mostly cuts acting when it is false. The newest Claude and GPT models always open a counted second record, then never act. When we add a same-name, same-zip customer to a retail benchmark, a lookup returning that customer first led to wrong-account writes in about a quarter of conversations, and one that checks a street the user knows kept completion near the one-customer level. Safe writes therefore need lookups that list or check competing records, and evaluations that vary what tools show.

items.title: Learn then Bet: Learning Interpretable Rules for Reliable Agent Intervention
items.description: Autonomous agents now run for hundreds of steps with little or no human supervision. In practice, practitioners use runtime monitors such as turn limits and keyword filters to decide when a run should be stopped, upgraded, or assisted. However, these heuristics may stop runs that would otherwise succeed or allow failing runs to continue. To address this limitation, we introduce LeBet (Learn then Bet), a statistical learning framework that derives its learning objective from sufficient conditions for valid and powerful intervention. In particular, LeBet learns an interpretable OR-of-AND monitor and accumulates evidence through a fixed betting statistic, intervening when the evidence reaches a prescribed threshold. Under finite within-class exchangeability and leave-one-out stability, we derive finite-sample guarantees for false-positive control (validity) and detection power conditional on the training data, using the same trajectories for learning and calibration without assuming independent and identically distributed trajectories. To address the intractable combinatorial optimization problem in our learning formulation, we use stochastic local search that leverages the monitor's Boolean structure to propose rule edits aimed at improving empirical separation. On SWE-bench Lite with Ministral 3 8B, the learned monitor saves $34.46\%$ of input-plus-output tokens and increases output precision from $18.33\%$ to $21.59\%$. The empirical false-positive rate is $13.64\%$. Our results show how to formalize the learning problem over interpretable rule sets with statistical conditions and establish training-conditional guarantees for reliable intervention based on partial histories.

items.title: Aligned, Conflicting, or Unspecified? A Diagnostic Benchmark for Multimodal Time Series Forecasting
items.description: Artificial Intelligence of Things (AIoT) systems increasingly combine sensed time series with external text such as expert reports and news, yet how reliably models use text that agrees or conflicts with the sensed history remains unclear. We introduce the first real-world diagnostic benchmark organized by text-history relationship: 1,762 text-window pairs across sensor telemetry (Weather), web-service traffic (Wikipedia), and market data streams (Finance), each labeled Aligned, Conflicting, or Unspecified by whether the text's direction agrees with the historical trend, opposes it, or is not stated. Across ten pretrained models evaluated zero-shot, we investigate text selection and combination under text-history relationships (RQ1) and error diagnosis and horizon-scaled revision control (RQ2). For RQ1, we compare two types of text on paired Weather windows: one directly forecasts temperature changes, while the other describes related weather conditions, such as winds and fronts. Under Aligned, the first type yields the lowest error for most models. Under Conflicting, it increases most models' error above the no-text baseline; we therefore add only its stated magnitude and timing to the second type. Compared with either type alone, this combination lowers mean absolute scaled error (MASE) for six models and raises directional accuracy (DA) for seven. For RQ2, an error decomposition attributes the error increase to oversized revisions, and a training-free rule that limits them outperforms forecasts both with and without text for the four models with this trade-off, lowering MASE by 4.49%-21.98% and raising DA by 2.99%-9.71%. Our dataset is available at https://github.com/Shelton1202/ACU-Bench.

items.title: OCTAVE: A Capability-Resolved Benchmark for End-to-End HTML5 Game Generation
items.description: Complete game generation requires agents to coordinate rules, interactions, states, and presentation over a long development process. A single aggregate score obscures which capabilities are implemented and which requirements remain unmet. We present OCTAVE, a benchmark for complete HTML5 game generation organized around eight Capability Dimensions, with 180 tasks and 1,800 Evaluation Requirements drawn from real player requests, commercial-mechanics reconstruction, and human expert design. It covers PC Web, Mobile Web, 2D, and 3D. Requirements distinguish Completeness, assessing publicly specified core implementation, from Richness, assessing hidden, deeper system relationships. Static source-code judgments provide requirement-level diagnosis across capabilities and task conditions. Evaluation of 11 model-harness combinations yields 33.2% Completeness and 32.5% Richness; 19.9% of generation records are static gate failures or missing artifacts. Excluding same-model self-evaluation, even the best combination remains below 50% on both public and hidden requirements. Richness is not harder than Completeness under every task condition. Systems perform relatively better on Core Rules and Numerical Design, while AI/NPC and Feedback and Game Feel show more prominent gaps. Requirement difficulty offers coarse stratification but is only weakly negatively correlated with pass rates. A limited human cross-check finds that requirements judged satisfied by humans but failed by the automated evaluator are the main direction of disagreement. OCTAVE extends evaluation beyond aggregate scores to diagnosis localized by requirement, capability, and task condition.

items.title: Co-Sight Harness: Externalized Control Assets and Deterministic Enforcement for Long-Horizon Business Agents
items.description: Long-horizon business workflows fail in two ways: errors accumulate as a chain of activities lengthens, and the knowledge an activity needs is written in a different vocabulary from the user's request. We study whether such workflows can be made reliable without changing the language model. Our method keeps the backbone fixed and moves the workflow definition, state and domain knowledge into versioned control assets outside the model. A state machine and machine-checkable acceptance gates enforce these assets during execution; an independent auditor grades the resulting trace. The assets are updated only after a regression check and human approval .We evaluate the method on three deployed workflows exceeding 200 steps. On Domain A, a 120-case end-to-end evaluation set shows unattended completion rising from 50% to 100%, retrieval recall from 56% to 91.67%, and end-to-end latency dropping from 440 to 159 minutes, with scenario-analysis recall rising from 45% to 93%. Two other domains were taken over by teams that did not write the assets, one in four days and one in seven days. A controlled ablation separates the two failure sources. The code is available at https://github.com/ZTE-AICloud/Co-Sight/tree/master/Co-Sight%20Harness.

items.title: An AI-enabled high-resolution chlorophyll-a forecasting model that outperforms the operational global biogeochemical system
items.description: Surface chlorophyll-a concentration is a key indicator of marine phytoplankton variability, and short-term forecasts of its distribution provide advance information for marine ecosystem monitoring and management. However, interactions between physical transport and biological processes complicate chlorophyll-a forecasting, and simulating these coupled processes with conventional numerical models imposes substantial computational demands. Here we introduce ChlCast, an AI model that generates daily forecasts of surface chlorophyll-a concentration over a 10-day horizon at approximately 4-km resolution between 60$^\circ$S and 60$^\circ$N. ChlCast combines factorized spatiotemporal convolutions with a multiscale architecture to learn from historical chlorophyll-a fields and climatological information. Compared with the operational 0.25$^\circ$ Copernicus global ocean biogeochemical forecasting system, ChlCast reduces mean absolute error and root mean square error by 70.74% and 47.63%, respectively, against satellite-derived Level-4 chlorophyll-a fields, and by 35.03% and 13.07% against independent BGC-Argo in situ observations.
